name: Japanese avant-garde fashion
summary: The black, loose and torn clothes that Rei Kawakubo, Yohji Yamamoto and Issey Miyake showed in Paris from 1981. The clothes are oversized, asymmetric and unfinished, with no wish to show the body.

philosophy.core_thesis: A garment is a space around the body, not a copy of it: it can be loose, torn, uneven and black, and still be beautiful.
design_principles: Cut the garment 20 to 40 cm wider than the body, so that it hangs in folds.
Wear black as the base, and use white, grey and indigo as the main other colours.
Leave an edge raw, a seam outside or a hem uneven.
Set a sleeve, a collar or a hem off the centre, so that the cut is asymmetric.
Make a cloth with texture: boiled wool, felt, a holed knit or a heat-set pleat.
Place a lump or a fold on the body, so that the outline changes.
Treat the cloth as the first idea and cut the garment from it.
anti_patterns: A tight, sexy waist and bust

silhouette.shape: A large, loose and often asymmetric shape that stands away from the body: a long coat, a wide trouser or a draped dress.
silhouette.line: A dropped shoulder, no waist, and a hem that is uneven or off the level.
silhouette.fit: Very loose; the body is hidden and the garment moves round it with room to spare.
silhouette.proportion: Garment 20 to 40 cm wider than the body. Hem at the calf or the ankle. A lopsided hem is 10 to 25 cm out of line.
rules: Remove the waist and the bust shaping.
Cut a coat or a dress as one large wrapped piece.
Leave a frayed or turned-out edge at the hem.
Use a hole, a twist or a fold to break the plain surface.
Pair the garment with a flat shoe.

fabrics.rule: Choose a cloth with texture and weight that hangs in folds: boiled wool, felt, plain jersey and black gabardine, in a dull finish.

methods: flat pattern from one large piece
construction.closures: Large hidden snaps, ties and wrap closures, or a single button; no waist closure.
construction.details: A single large pocket, a dropped sleeve, a seam on the outside, a hanging flap and a hole in the knit.

surface.pattern: Plain black, white or grey; texture from the weave; sometimes holes and lumps that make a pattern.
surface.gloss: Wool and felt at 1–4 GU; cotton at 2–6 GU; the style avoids a high gloss.
surface.wear: The style likes a worn and unfinished surface: a frayed edge, a faded black and a wrinkled cloth.

palette.strategy: Black first, then white, grey and indigo; colour appears only in small, flat blocks.

processes: flat pattern cutting in the studio
weaving and dyeing of custom cloth
making.scale: Designer ready-to-wear in small runs, shown in Paris twice each year, with a large amount of made-to-order cloth.
making.signs: Raw edges, outside seams, a heavy fall, and a cloth that the maker wove or knitted to order.

pieces.form: Large wrapped dress with a lopsided hem
Long coat with no waist and a dropped shoulder
Loose knit with holes and an uneven hem
Wide black trousers with a dropped crotch
Oversized shirt with an off-centre opening

canonical_works.work: Body Meets Dress, Dress Meets Body

emotion.target_response: A quiet shock and a sense of thought: the viewer sees a dark, loose form that asks what a garment is for.

use_cases: a costume for a dark, quiet film
a collection brief with sculptural cut
a study note on 1980s Paris fashion
avoid_when: the brief wants a sexy, fitted or glamorous look
the brief wants bright colour or ornament
the brief wants a clean, neat uniform

modifiers.how: Keep the loose cut and the dark palette, remove the raw edges and the holes, and finish each seam.
Keep the black and the tears, add leather and pins, and shorten the shape.
